questions.q: Why isn't workload-level Kubernetes portability enough to make an application cloud-portable on its own?
options: Because Kubernetes Deployments cannot run on more than one cloud at a time
Because if application code calls a cloud SDK like boto3 or ServiceBusClient directly, the business logic is welded to that one provider regardless of where the container runs
Because Kubernetes does not support environment variables
Because every cloud requires a completely different programming language for its SDKs
questions.explain: Portability at the orchestration layer doesn't help if the application's own code directly imports and calls a cloud-specific SDK — that coupling exists independent of where the container is scheduled.

questions.q: In the MessageQueue interface example, what does application business logic actually call?
options: queue.send(payload) against the MessageQueue interface, never a cloud SDK method directly
sqs.send_message(...) directly, since that is the only method available
ServiceBusClient.from_connection_string(...) every time a message needs to be sent
A GraphQL endpoint that wraps both Service Bus and SQS
questions.explain: Business logic depends only on the MessageQueue interface's send/receive/ack methods; which concrete adapter (AzureServiceBusQueue or SqsQueue) is behind that call is decided elsewhere, not in the calling code.

questions.q: Where does the decision of which cloud adapter to instantiate (Azure Service Bus vs. AWS SQS) typically live?
options: Scattered across every file that needs to send a message
Hardcoded separately into each business-logic function
In a single factory function that reads configuration (like an environment variable) and returns the right concrete adapter
Inside the Kubernetes Deployment's readiness probe
questions.explain: A factory function centralizes the provider decision in one place, typically based on an environment variable like CLOUD_PROVIDER, so the rest of the codebase only ever depends on the interface.

questions.q: What is a real cost of abstracting a cloud service behind a common interface, according to this lesson?
options: It is always free and has no downsides whatsoever
It automatically improves application performance on every cloud
It eliminates the need for integration testing entirely

The interface narrows to the lowest common denominator, so a provider-specific feature like SQS FIFO deduplication or Service Bus sessions can't be fully exposed without the abstraction becoming leaky
questions.explain: An interface built to work with multiple providers can only expose the capabilities common to all of them; features unique to one provider either get left out or leak through, undermining the abstraction.

questions.q: When does building a clean adapter-pattern interface for a cloud service actually pay for itself?
options: Only when you will genuinely use more than one concrete implementation — otherwise it's overhead with no real payoff
Always, for every single cloud dependency in any application, with no exceptions
Only for compute workloads, never for queues or databases
Only when the team has fewer than two engineers
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that building and maintaining a clean interface and multiple adapters is a bet on an actual multi-cloud deployment or future migration — for a workload that will only ever run on one cloud, it's pure added cost.
